questions.q: Memory safety means ensuring that attackers cannot read or write memory locations other than the ones the programmer intended.
questions.explain: That is the definition: memory safety keeps attackers from reading or writing memory the programmer did not intend to be accessed.

questions.q: After configuration errors, what is probably the largest single class of security errors exploited in practice?
questions.explain: Implementation errors (software security flaws) are probably the largest class after configuration errors. A system can have a perfect design and still be broken by its implementation.

questions.q: If a system has a perfect design, a perfect specification, and perfect algorithms, it cannot have implementation vulnerabilities.
questions.explain: Software security is about flaws in the implementation itself. A perfect design can still be implemented with exploitable bugs.

questions.q: Why is C the natural language for studying memory-safety vulnerabilities and defenses?
choices: C is not memory-safe, and many security-critical applications are written in it
C checks every array access at runtime, so its failures are easy to study
C programs cannot be compiled to x86
C has garbage collection, which causes most memory bugs
questions.explain: C is not a memory-safe language, and a lot of security-critical software is written in C. That combination makes its memory-safety bugs important.

questions.q: Which of these is a memory-safety violation?
choices: A firewall left in its default configuration
A protocol whose design lets anyone replay old messages
Input that makes a program write to memory the programmer never meant it to write
A user picking a weak password
questions.explain: Memory safety is specifically about reads and writes to unintended memory locations. The other options are configuration, design, or user problems.

questions.q: How many bytes long is the bit string 1000100010001000?
questions.explain: It has 16 bits, and 1 byte = 8 bits, so it is 2 bytes.

questions.q: Convert 0b1011111011101111 to hexadecimal.
questions.explain: Split into groups of 4 bits: 1011 = B, 1110 = E, 1110 = E, 1111 = F, which gives 0xBEEF.

questions.q: Convert 0xA5 to binary (8 bits).
questions.explain: Each hex digit is 4 bits: A = 1010 and 5 = 0101, so 0xA5 = 0b10100101.

questions.q: How many bits does a single hexadecimal digit represent?
questions.explain: Each hex digit stands for one of 16 values, which is exactly 4 bits (0000 to 1111).

questions.q: What determines the size of a "word"?
choices: The size of a pointer, which depends on the CPU architecture
The size of one hexadecimal digit
questions.explain: A word is the size of a pointer, so it depends on the architecture. On a 32-bit architecture a word is 32 bits.

questions.q: On a 32-bit architecture, how many bytes are in one word?
questions.explain: A word is 32 bits, and 32 / 8 = 4 bytes.

questions.q: Which prefixes mark binary and hexadecimal strings?
questions.explain: 0b comes before binary strings (0b1010) and 0x comes before hexadecimal strings (0xA).

questions.q: In what order do these steps happen when a C program goes from source code to running?
questions.explain: The compiler turns C into assembly, the assembler turns assembly into machine code, the linker resolves external libraries and outputs an executable, and the loader sets up memory and runs it.

questions.q: Which tool translates assembly instructions into machine code (raw bits)?
questions.explain: The assembler converts assembly instructions into machine code.

questions.q: Which tool resolves dependencies on external libraries and outputs a binary executable?
questions.explain: The linker resolves external library dependencies and produces the final executable.

questions.q: When a user runs an executable, what sets up an address space in memory and runs the machine code?
questions.explain: The loader creates the program's address space and starts executing its machine code.

questions.q: What does the compiler produce from C source code?
questions.explain: The compiler translates C code into assembly instructions (x86 here). The assembler then turns those into machine code.

questions.q: From lowest address to highest address, what is the order of the four sections of a running C program's address space?
questions.explain: Code is at the lowest addresses, then static, then heap (growing up), and the stack is at the highest addresses (growing down).

questions.q: Which section holds global variables, static variables, and constants?
questions.explain: The static section holds constants, static variables, and global variables.

questions.q: Memory returned by malloc lives in which section?
questions.explain: Dynamically allocated memory from malloc is on the heap. It stays allocated until free is called.

questions.q: Which section holds local variables and other information about function calls?
questions.explain: The stack holds local variables and per-call data such as saved registers and arguments.

questions.q: In the address space, each bit of memory has its own unique address.
questions.explain: Addresses are per byte, not per bit. Each byte has a unique address.

questions.q: How many bytes are in the address space of a 32-bit system? Give the exact number.
questions.explain: Addresses are 32 bits long, so there are 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 byte addresses, from 0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF.

questions.q: How big is the address space of a 64-bit system?
questions.explain: Addresses are 64 bits long and each address names one byte, so the space is 2^64 bytes.

questions.q: Which statements about how the heap and stack grow are true?
choices: The heap starts at lower addresses and grows up toward higher addresses
On the heap, older allocations have lower addresses
The stack starts at higher addresses and grows down as more functions are called
A new local variable on the stack has a higher address than earlier ones
On the stack, older variables have lower addresses
questions.explain: The heap grows up, so older allocations sit lower. The stack grows down, so newer locals get lower addresses and older ones sit higher.

questions.q: The first member of a struct is stored at the lowest address of the struct.
questions.explain: Struct members are laid out with the first member at the lowest address, even when the struct is on the stack.

questions.q: When memory is drawn as a grid of bytes, where is address 0x00000000?
questions.explain: Addresses increase from left to right and from bottom to top, so 0x00000000 is at the bottom-left and 0xFFFFFFFF is at the top-right.

questions.q: On x86, the word 0x44332211 is stored starting at address 0x1000. Which byte is at address 0x1000?
questions.explain: x86 is little-endian: the least significant byte (0x11) goes at the lowest address and the most significant byte (0x44) at the highest.

questions.q: On x86, the word 0xDEADBEEF is stored at addresses 0x2000 through 0x2003. Which byte is at address 0x2003?
questions.explain: In little-endian order the bytes are 0xEF, 0xBE, 0xAD, 0xDE from 0x2000 up to 0x2003. The most significant byte, 0xDE, is at the highest address.

questions.q: On x86, memory holds the bytes 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12 at four increasing addresses. What word is read from the lowest of those addresses?
questions.explain: In little-endian order the byte at the lowest address (0x78) is the least significant, so the word is 0x12345678.

questions.q: If the word 0x44332211 were stored in big-endian format instead, which byte would be at the lowest address?
questions.explain: Big-endian puts the least significant byte at the highest address, so the most significant byte (0x44) is at the lowest address.

questions.q: Networking protocols are often big-endian.
questions.explain: Unlike x86, many networking protocols use big-endian byte order.

questions.q: When a memory diagram shows whole 4-byte words in each row instead of individual bytes, the bytes are no longer stored in little-endian order.
questions.explain: Writing words on a diagram only hides little-endianness to make it easier to read. The bytes in memory are still stored little-endian.

questions.q: What does the eip register store?
choices: The address of the top of the current stack frame
The address of the bottom of the current stack frame
The address of the machine instruction currently being executed
The return value of the last function call
questions.explain: eip is the instruction pointer. It holds the address of the current instruction, like the PC in RISC-V.

questions.q: What does the ebp register store?
choices: The address of the top (highest address) of the current stack frame
The address of the bottom (lowest address) of the current stack frame
The address of the current instruction
The address of the start of the heap
questions.explain: ebp is the base pointer. It points to the top of the current stack frame, which is the frame's highest address.

questions.q: What does the esp register store?
choices: The address of the top (highest address) of the current stack frame
The address of the bottom (lowest address) of the current stack frame
The address of the current instruction
The size of the current stack frame
questions.explain: esp is the stack pointer. It points to the bottom of the current stack frame, which is the frame's lowest address.

questions.q: Which pairs of an x86 register and its RISC-V counterpart are correct?
questions.explain: eip is the program counter (PC), esp is the stack pointer (SP), and ebp is the frame pointer (FP). RISC-V often uses FP as the general-purpose register s0.

questions.q: Which section of memory does eip usually point to?
questions.explain: eip points to instructions, and instructions are stored in the code section.

questions.q: Which section of memory do ebp and esp usually point to?
questions.explain: ebp and esp mark the top and bottom of the current stack frame, so they point into the stack.

questions.q: Like bytes of memory, x86 registers each have a numeric address.
questions.explain: Registers live on the CPU and have no addresses. They are referred to by name (eip, ebp, esp, eax, ...). Each one holds one word (4 bytes).

questions.q: What does the "e" at the start of eip, ebp, and esp stand for?
questions.explain: "e" stands for extended. It shows the registers are the 32-bit versions of the original 16-bit registers.

questions.q: What does the x86 push instruction do?
choices: Increments esp, then stores the value in the space just freed
Decrements esp to allocate space, then stores the value in that new space
Stores the value at ebp and leaves esp unchanged
Copies the value at esp into a register
questions.explain: The stack grows down, so push first decrements esp to make room and then writes the value there.

questions.q: esp is 0x1000. After a 4-byte value is pushed, what is esp, and where is the value stored?
questions.explain: push decrements esp by 4 to 0x0FFC and then stores the value at the new esp, 0x0FFC.

questions.q: What does the x86 pop instruction do?
choices: Copies the value at the bottom of the stack into a register and increments esp
Erases the value at the bottom of the stack and decrements esp
Decrements esp and copies a register onto the stack
questions.explain: pop copies the value at esp into a register and increments esp, which removes the value from the stack.

questions.q: When a value is popped off the stack, it is erased from memory.
questions.explain: The bytes stay in memory. Only esp moves up, so the old value is now below esp, in undefined memory.

questions.q: esp is 0x0FFC and `pop %eax` runs. Which statements are true afterward?
choices: eax holds the 4-byte value that was at 0x0FFC
The bytes at 0x0FFC still hold the popped value
The memory at 0x0FFC is now considered undefined
questions.explain: pop copies the value at esp into eax and increments esp by 4 to 0x1000. The bytes at 0x0FFC are not cleared, but they are below esp now, so they are undefined.

questions.q: How should memory on the stack below esp be treated?
choices: As part of the current stack frame
As holding the caller's local variables
questions.explain: esp marks the bottom of the stack, so anything below it is undefined. Popping and freeing a frame (moving esp up) work this way.

questions.q: What does `addl $0x8, %ebx` do?
questions.explain: In AT&T syntax the destination comes last. The source is the immediate $0x8 and the destination is %ebx, so EBX = EBX + 0x8.

questions.q: What does `xorl 4(%esi), %eax` do?
questions.explain: 4(%esi) is a memory reference: the value at the address 4 bytes above ESI. The destination is %eax, so EAX = EAX ^ *(ESI + 4).

questions.q: In AT&T x86 syntax, what does a `$` prefix mean, as in `$0x4`?
questions.explain: Immediates (constants) start with $. Registers start with %, and memory references use parentheses.

questions.q: In AT&T x86 syntax, what does `12(%esp)` refer to?
choices: The memory 12 bytes below the address in esp
The memory 12 bytes above the address in esp
questions.explain: Parentheses dereference memory, and the number in front is added to the address. So 12(%esp) is the memory at esp + 12.

questions.q: In AT&T x86 syntax, the destination operand comes last, which is the opposite of RISC-V assembly.
questions.explain: AT&T syntax writes source then destination. RISC-V writes the destination first.

questions.q: Every x86 instruction is exactly 4 bytes long.
questions.explain: x86 instructions have variable length, from 1 to 16 bytes.

questions.q: Inside a function after its prologue has run, what does `movl 8(%ebp), %eax` do?
choices: Stores eax into the memory 8 bytes above ebp
Loads the function's first argument into eax
Loads the saved frame pointer (sfp) into eax
questions.explain: The source is the memory at ebp + 8 and the destination is eax. ebp points at the sfp, ebp + 4 holds the rip, and ebp + 8 holds the first argument.

questions.q: How does Intel x86 syntax differ from AT&T syntax?
choices: Intel syntax reverses the order of source and destination
Intel syntax has no memory references
Intel syntax uses % before every immediate
There is no difference, only the name
questions.explain: Intel syntax reverses source and destination. Percent signs before register names usually mean you are reading AT&T syntax.

questions.q: What does `(%esp)` mean when no offset is written before the parentheses?
choices: The memory at the address in esp, with an implicit offset of 0
questions.explain: Without an offset, the parentheses dereference the address in esp directly, which is the same as an offset of 0.

questions.q: Like RISC-V, x86 passes function arguments in registers.
questions.explain: x86 passes arguments by pushing them onto the stack. RISC-V passes them in registers.

questions.q: main calls foo(1, 2). Which argument is pushed onto the stack first?
choices: Both are pushed at the same time
questions.explain: Arguments are pushed in reverse order, so 2 (the last argument) is pushed first and 1 is pushed second.

questions.q: After a function's arguments are pushed, which argument is at the lowest address?
questions.explain: Arguments are pushed in reverse order and the stack grows down, so the first argument ends up at the lowest address.

questions.q: What is the rip saved on the stack during a function call?
choices: The caller's old eip, so execution can return to the caller
questions.explain: The rip (return instruction pointer, or old eip) is pushed before eip is changed to the callee, so execution can resume in the caller.

questions.q: What is the sfp saved on the stack during a function call?
choices: The caller's old ebp (saved frame pointer)
A pointer to the static section
questions.explain: The sfp (saved frame pointer) is the old ebp. It is pushed before ebp is moved to the new frame.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the first six steps of an x86 function call?
choices: Push args -> push old eip (rip) -> update eip -> push old ebp (sfp) -> move ebp down -> move esp down
Push old eip (rip) -> push args -> update eip -> move ebp down -> push old ebp (sfp) -> move esp down
Push args -> update eip -> push old eip (rip) -> push old ebp (sfp) -> move esp down -> move ebp down
Push old ebp (sfp) -> push args -> push old eip (rip) -> update eip -> move esp down -> move ebp down
questions.explain: Each register's old value is saved before it is overwritten: args, then rip, then update eip, then sfp, then ebp moves down to esp, then esp moves down to make room for locals.

questions.q: Inside a callee after its prologue, the first argument is at address ebp + ___ (in bytes).
questions.explain: ebp points at the sfp (4 bytes), ebp + 4 is the rip (4 bytes), so the first argument starts at ebp + 8.

questions.q: A callee takes two 4-byte int arguments. After its prologue, the second argument is at address ebp + ___ (in bytes).
questions.explain: The first argument is at ebp + 8 and takes 4 bytes. The second argument comes right after it, at a higher address, at ebp + 12.

questions.q: After a function's prologue, what is stored at the address ebp points to, and at ebp + 4?
choices: ebp: the rip; ebp + 4: the sfp
ebp: the sfp; ebp + 4: the rip
ebp: the first local variable; ebp + 4: the first argument
ebp: the first argument; ebp + 4: the second argument
questions.explain: The sfp was pushed last before ebp was set to esp, so ebp points at the sfp. The rip was pushed just before it, at ebp + 4.

questions.q: Which list shows a callee's stack contents from highest address to lowest?
questions.explain: Things pushed earlier are at higher addresses: the arguments, then the rip, then the sfp. The local variables go in the space below them.

questions.q: eip and ebp are saved on the stack during a call. Why isn't the old esp saved too?
choices: esp is never changed during a function call
esp is saved in ebp automatically by the call instruction
esp moves down as values are pushed and back up as they are removed, so it returns to its old position by itself
questions.explain: Each push moves esp down and each removal moves it back up. When the call finishes, esp is back where it started.

questions.q: The rip pushed during a call is the address of the call instruction itself.
questions.explain: The value pushed is the current eip advanced by one instruction, so after the return, execution continues with the instruction right after the call.

questions.q: When a function is ready to return, it first moves esp up to ebp. What does that do?
choices: It frees the function's local variables, because they are now below esp
It jumps back to the caller
It removes the arguments from the stack
questions.explain: Moving esp up to ebp puts the locals below esp, so they are now undefined. The sfp and rip are then popped, and the caller removes the arguments last.

questions.q: Of the 11 steps of an x86 function call and return, which ones run in the caller?
questions.explain: The caller pushes the arguments, saves the rip, and changes eip (steps 1-3). The callee runs steps 4-10. After the return, the caller removes the arguments (step 11).

questions.q: What does `call foo` do?
choices: Pushes the old eip (rip) onto the stack and sets eip to the start of foo
Pushes the old ebp (sfp) and sets ebp to esp
Pushes foo's arguments onto the stack
questions.explain: call does steps 2-3: it saves the return address (rip) on the stack and then jumps by changing eip to foo's code.

questions.q: The `leave` instruction is shorthand for which instructions?
questions.explain: leave combines steps 8 and 9: it moves esp back up to ebp and then pops the sfp back into ebp.

questions.q: The `ret` instruction is shorthand for which step?
choices: pop %eip, which restores the old eip (rip)
pop %ebp, which restores the old ebp (sfp)
mov %ebp, %esp, which frees the local variables
questions.explain: ret is step 10: it pops the rip off the stack into eip, so execution returns to the caller.

questions.q: Which instruction sequence is a function prologue?
questions.explain: The prologue is steps 4-6: save the old ebp, move ebp down to esp, and move esp down to allocate the frame. The second option is the epilogue.

questions.q: Which steps make up the function epilogue?
choices: Steps 8-10: move esp up, restore the old ebp, restore the old eip
Steps 4-6: push the sfp, move ebp down, move esp down
Steps 1-3: push args, push the rip, update eip
questions.explain: The epilogue is steps 8-10, usually written as `leave` followed by `ret`.

questions.q: Which instruction moves ebp down to where esp points (step 5)?
questions.explain: In AT&T syntax the source is first, so `mov %esp, %ebp` copies esp into ebp. `mov %ebp, %esp` does the reverse and is step 8.

questions.q: A caller pushes three 4-byte int arguments and then calls a function. After the function returns, the caller runs `add $N, %esp` to remove the arguments. What is N?
questions.explain: Three 4-byte arguments take 12 bytes, so esp has to move up by 12. For two arguments, as in foo(1, 2), it is `add $8, %esp`.

questions.q: In the prologue instruction `sub $16, %esp`, what decides the number 16?
choices: The compiler, based on how much space the function's locals and other data need
It is always 16 for every function
questions.explain: The compiler picks how far to move esp down. A function with a big local array needs more space than one with a few small locals.

questions.q: main calls foo(1, 2), where foo has a prologue of `push %ebp; mov %esp, %ebp; sub $16, %esp`. Just before main pushes the arguments, esp = 0xbfff0100. What is ebp after foo's prologue finishes?
questions.explain: push $2 -> esp 0xbfff00fc; push $1 -> 0xbfff00f8; call pushes the rip -> 0xbfff00f4; push %ebp -> 0xbfff00f0; mov %esp, %ebp -> ebp = 0xbfff00f0.

questions.q: Same setup: main calls foo(1, 2), esp = 0xbfff0100 before the arguments are pushed, and foo's prologue ends with `sub $16, %esp`. What is esp after the prologue?
questions.explain: esp reaches 0xbfff00f0 after the args, rip, and sfp are pushed. Subtracting 16 (0x10) gives 0xbfff00e0.

questions.q: Same setup: main calls foo(1, 2) with esp = 0xbfff0100 before the arguments are pushed. At what address is foo's first argument, a = 1?
questions.explain: 1 was pushed second, so it is at 0xbfff00f8. That equals ebp + 8 = 0xbfff00f0 + 8. The 2 is at 0xbfff00fc and the rip is at 0xbfff00f4.

questions.q: Same setup: esp = 0xbfff0100 before main pushes foo's two arguments. After foo returns and main runs `add $8, %esp`, what is esp?
questions.explain: leave and ret bring esp back to 0xbfff00f8 (just above the rip), and add $8 removes the two arguments, so esp is back at 0xbfff0100. That is why esp never needs to be saved.
